title: Outer-horn restriction on equivalence-edge components of a Segal space
statement:
Use small simplicial sets, Kan complexes, homotopy fibers and weak homotopy equivalences from [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], the Kan model structure of [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper], and the Reedy model structure of [lem-coef-reedy-model-structure]. A simplicial space is a functor $V:\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathrm{sSet}$. It is a Segal space if it is Reedy fibrant and its consecutive-edge maps $V_n\to V_1\times_{V_0}\cdots\times_{V_0}V_1$ are weak homotopy equivalences for every $n\geq2$. For vertices $x,y$ of $V_0$, let $M_V(x,y)$ be the strict fiber of $(d_1,d_0):V_1\to V_0^2$. The homotopy category $hV$ has those vertices as objects, morphisms $\pi_0M_V(x,y)$, identity from $s_0$, and composition from the degree-two Segal map and $d_1$. Let $V_{\mathrm{eq}}\subseteq V_1$ be the union of components representing isomorphisms in $hV$.

For $n\geq0$ let $F(n)_k=\operatorname{Hom}_\Delta([k],[n])$, discrete in the inner direction. Let $cK$ denote the constant simplicial space on a simplicial set $K$. For a small simplicial space $X$, define the simplicial mapping space by
$$\operatorname{Map}(X,V)_q=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{sS}}(X\times c\Delta^q,V),$$
with simplicial operators given by precomposition. Define $T_V(X)\subseteq\operatorname{Map}(X,V)$ to be the intersection of the inverse images of $V_{\mathrm{eq}}\subseteq V_1=\operatorname{Map}(F(1),V)$ under restriction along every map $F(1)\to X$. Thus a simplex belongs to $T_V(X)$ exactly when all its edge evaluations belong to $V_{\mathrm{eq}}$.

For an integer $k\geq2$, let $H(k)\subseteq F(k)$ be the union of the faces $d^iF(k-1)$ for $1\leq i\leq k$; equivalently, in outer degree $m$ it consists of those monotone maps $[m]\to[k]$ whose image omits at least one vertex other than $0$. For every Segal space $V$ and every $k\geq2$, restriction induces a weak homotopy equivalence
$$T_V(F(k))\longrightarrow T_V(H(k)).$$

source.place: Section 11, Lemma 11.10, with H(k) and the equivalence-edge mapping subspaces defined in Section 11.7 immediately before it; printed pp. 26-27. Read online; archival copy WANTED. No Stacks tag states this result.

proof.text: First record the mapping-space facts needed throughout. Restriction along every inclusion $A\subseteq B$ of the finite discrete simplicial spaces below is a Kan fibration by [lem-coef-segal-cartesian-exponent], and each unrestricted mapping space is Kan (apply the same result to $\varnothing\subseteq B$). By [lem-coef-segal-homotopy-category-components], invertibility is constant on components of $V_1$. Each $T_V(B)$ is therefore a union of components of $\operatorname{Map}(B,V)$: along a path every edge evaluation stays in its component. Such a union is Kan, and restriction between these unions is still a Kan fibration, because every horn has a vertex and a filler lies in the component of that vertex. Whenever $T_V(B)$ is the inverse image of $T_V(A)$, the restricted map is exactly a pullback. The Segal restriction to the consecutive-edge spine is a trivial Kan fibration: it is a Kan fibration by restriction and a weak equivalence by the Segal hypothesis, hence trivial in [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper]. This remains true after fixing all vertices or selecting invertible components, when the selected source is the full inverse image. All edges of a simplex are composites in $hV$ of its consecutive edges, by restricting to its triangles; thus selecting all invertible edges is equivalent to selecting its consecutive edges.

source.place: Sections 2.5,4.1,5.3-5.8 and 11.7; explicit component and horn-lifting argument

proof.text: Prove the base case $k=2$. The horn $H(2)$ is the union of edges $01$ and $02$, glued at vertex $0$, so its all-equivalence mapping space has, over vertices $(x,y,z)$, the fiber $M(x,y)_{\mathrm{eq}}\times M(x,z)_{\mathrm{eq}}$. The corresponding fiber for $F(2)$ is the subspace $Z$ of $M(x,y,z)$ with all three edges invertible. Project both spaces to $M(x,y)_{\mathrm{eq}}$ by the edge $01$. These projections are Kan fibrations by step 1 and the product projection; the induced fiber map at an invertible $f:x\to y$ is $d_1:Z_f\to M(x,z)_{\mathrm{eq}}$. The map $d_0:Z_f\to M(y,z)_{\mathrm{eq}}$ is a trivial Kan fibration, being the pullback of the degree-two Segal restriction to the spine. Here the missing edge $02$ is invertible exactly when $12$ is invertible, since $[02]=[12][f]$. By [lem-coef-segal-composition-equivalences], $d_1$ on this fiber is homotopic to $f^*d_0$, and $f^*$ is a weak equivalence preserving and reflecting invertible components. Its restriction to these unions is a weak equivalence: its bijection on components restricts to the invertible ones, and its based homotopy-group isomorphisms do not change when the other components are removed. The homotopy restricted to $Z_f$ lands in $M(x,z)_{\mathrm{eq}}$: for every source vertex its path begins at the invertible edge $d_1$, and each image simplex lies in that same selected union of components. Realize this restricted homotopy using [lem-coef-simplicial-realization-cylinder]; [lem-coef-homotopy-groups-basepoint-change] says that continuously homotopic realizations have the same weak-equivalence property. Hence $d_1$ is a weak equivalence. Apply [lem-coef-kan-fibration-arbitrary-base-fibers] first over $M(x,y)_{\mathrm{eq}}$, and then over $V_0^3$. The latter projections are Kan fibrations by restriction to the vertices. This proves $T_V(F(2))\to T_V(H(2))$ is a weak equivalence. The same reasoning includes empty fibers and an empty $V$.

source.place: Sections 11.2-11.6; expanded proof of the degree-two case of Lemma 11.10

proof.text: For the induction, fix $k\geq3$ and assume restriction $\rho_{k-1}:T_V(F(k-1))\to T_V(H(k-1))$ is a weak equivalence. It is also a Kan fibration by step 1, hence a trivial Kan fibration by [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper]. Define $C(k)\subseteq F(k)$ to consist of simplices whose vertex image does not contain the entire subset $\{2,\ldots,k\}$. Then $H(k)=C(k)\cup d^1F(k-1)$ and $C(k)\cap d^1F(k-1)=d^1H(k-1)$: the first union adds the subsets missing $1$, and within that face the forbidden subset is precisely its face opposite $0$. These equalities hold for every monotone map, so they are equalities of simplicial subobjects. Mapping out gives a strict pullback square, also after imposing the all-edge condition, since the edges of a union are the union of the edges. Thus $a:T_V(H(k))\to T_V(C(k))$ is the pullback of $\rho_{k-1}$ along restriction to $d^1H(k-1)$. It is a trivial Kan fibration: any boundary lifting problem projects to one for $\rho_{k-1}$, and the lifted simplex pairs with the prescribed simplex on $C(k)$.

source.place: Section 11.7, equality (11.9) and Lemma 11.10; degreewise verification of the gluing

proof.text: Put $A(k)=d^0H(k-1)\cup F(\{0,1\})\subseteq C(k)$, where the copy $d^0H(k-1)$ has vertices $1,\ldots,k$. Cover $C(k)$ by the full faces $F(S_J)$, where $S_J=\{0,1\}\cup J$ and $J$ ranges over all proper subsets of $\{2,\ldots,k\}$, including $J=\varnothing$. Every simplex of $C(k)$ belongs to one of these faces, by taking $J$ to be its image intersected with $\{2,\ldots,k\}$. The family is finite and closed under intersections, since $S_J\cap S_L=S_{J\cap L}$. On each face the intersection with $A(k)$ is exactly $F(\{0,1\})\cup F(\{1\}\cup J)$. These two subfaces are consecutive intervals for the induced order on $S_J$ and together contain its entire spine; for $J=\varnothing$ the intersection is the whole edge. The hypotheses of [lem-coef-segal-finite-cover-descent] hold. Consequently $b:\operatorname{Map}(C(k),V)\to\operatorname{Map}(A(k),V)$ is a trivial Kan fibration.

source.place: Lemma 11.11, proof; explicit finite face family and each interval-cover intersection

proof.text: The inverse image of $T_V(A(k))$ under $b$ is exactly $T_V(C(k))$. Indeed on every $F(S_J)$ all consecutive edges lie in $A(k)$, so invertibility on $A(k)$ makes each of its other edges invertible by the triangle composition relation in $hV$. Every edge of $C(k)$ lies in such a face. The converse follows by restriction. This checks the equality on vertices; it holds on every inner simplex because these spaces are unions of components. It follows that the restricted $b:T_V(C(k))\to T_V(A(k))$ is a pullback of the trivial fibration from step 4, and is itself trivial by the boundary-lifting argument of step 3.

source.place: Lemma 11.11 and the all-equivalence restriction in the last sentence of the proof of Lemma 11.10

proof.text: Let $B(k)=d^0F(k-1)\cup F(\{0,1\})$. Restriction $u:T_V(F(k))\to T_V(B(k))$ is a weak equivalence. To see this using exactly the Segal hypotheses, restrict both spaces further to the full consecutive spine $G(k)$. The restriction from $F(k)$ is the degree-$k$ Segal trivial fibration from step 1. The restriction from $B(k)$ is the pullback, after adjoining edge $01$ at vertex $1$, of the degree-$(k-1)$ Segal trivial fibration on $d^0F(k-1)$. The all-edge condition is exactly the inverse image of the all-invertible spine condition, since long edges in that face are composites. Both maps to $T_V(G(k))$ are therefore weak equivalences; two-out-of-three in [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper] proves the claim for $u$. Also $T_V(B(k))\to T_V(A(k))$ is a pullback of $\rho_{k-1}$, after adjoining the same edge $01$ at vertex $1$, because $d^0H(k-1)$ and $d^0F(k-1)$ both meet this edge in that vertex. Thus this second restriction is trivial. The composite $s:T_V(F(k))\to T_V(A(k))$ is a weak equivalence.

source.place: Proof of Lemma 11.10, last displayed comparison; written with the copy d^0H(k-1) used in the proof of Lemma 11.11

proof.text: Let $r:T_V(F(k))\to T_V(H(k))$ be the desired restriction. Precomposition identities give $s=b\,a\,r$, with $a,b$ from steps 3 and 5. Those two maps and $s$ are weak equivalences. Two-out-of-three in [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper] gives that $r$ is a weak equivalence. Step 2 supplies the base $k=2$, and steps 3-7 give the induction for each $k\geq3$, proving the statement for every $k\geq2$. No completeness of $V$ was used.
